rv.q: “Why are you so afraid of adults?” she asks, deadpan. Age-inappropriate danger lurks everywhere: The group will soon be commiserating with their friend Sophie (Sophie Rossman), who has been sexually menaced by a creep who turns out to be her father’s work buddy.
Amid the warmth and humor of her portrait of teenagehood, Smith is touching on a cold and bracing thing.

Doth the lady protest too much? Who hasn’t scribbled a “Do Not Come In” sign in a fit of rage, desperately hoping someone disregards the text in favor of subtext? What makes Smith’s writing especially satisfying is how she never succumbs to the urge to turn any of that subtext into text.
Eliya Smith's play about four teenaged girls is raw and messy and heartbreaking and joyful all at once.

The play is a melange of small talk, gossip, and sims for a third of its 90-odd minutes, until real life—in the form of a dangerous encounter with someone else’s dad—shakes up the characters and most of the audience as well. One of the girls is apparently the victim of abuse.

cn.t: Critics praise Eliya Smith's raw, unnerving portrait of teenage girls at sleepovers as messy, heartbreaking, and joyful, capturing the intensity of adolescence with authenticity and dark humor.
